t: Length of the Longest Increasing Path Through a Fixed Point
o: We need the longest chain of points with strictly increasing x and y that contains coordinates[k]. Any such path splits into a strictly-smaller part ending at k and a strictly-larger part starting at k, so the answer is (LIS ending at k) + (LIS starting at k) - 1. Example 1: below (2,2) only (0,0) qualifies (length 1); above it, (5,3) gives length 1; total 3. With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) DP is too slow, so we use the classic sort-by-x-then-patience-sorting LIS on the filtered points.
k: Split the problem at k: longest chain ending at k plus longest chain starting at k, minus 1 for double-counting k.

a.i: Compute dp1[i] = longest increasing chain ending at i and dp2[i] = longest decreasing-to-i chain starting at i using pairwise comparisons; answer = dp1[k] + dp2[k] - 1. Clear but too slow for n = 1e5; useful to establish correctness.
s: For i <= k, dp1[i] = 1 + max(dp1[j]) over j with both coordinates smaller.
Symmetrically compute dp2 for i >= k going right-to-left.
a.t: O(n^2) — pairwise DP transitions; will TLE at n = 1e5 but is correct.
a.sp: O(n) for the two DP arrays.

a.i: Only points strictly below k in both coordinates can precede k, and only points strictly above can follow it — filter them out first. On each filtered set, sort by x ascending and y descending (the tie-break prevents chaining equal-x points), then run the O(n log n) patience-sorting LIS on y. Strictness in y is preserved because bisect_left replaces equal values rather than extending.
s: Collect points with x < kx and y < ky into 'low', and x > kx, y > ky into 'high'.
Sort each by (x asc, y desc).
Run LIS (lower_bound on tails of y) on each list.
a.t: O(n log n) — filtering is linear, sorting and patience LIS are n log n.
a.sp: O(n) for the filtered lists and tails array.

w: Always decompose through the mandatory point first — it turns one hard problem into two standard LIS problems. Pitfalls: forgetting strict inequality when filtering (points sharing x or y with k cannot be used), and forgetting the y-descending tie-break when sorting by x (otherwise equal-x points chain incorrectly). Follow-up: report the actual path, or handle queries for many k values.
